title: Fur, Feathers and Scales: Parent Guide
endLine: Each animal's covering fits where it lives and how it moves.

scenes.tts: Why does a feather feel smooth one way and rough the other? Fish scales can feel that way, too. At the kitchen table, your child can compare animal coverings and use what they notice to sort pictures.
scenes.caption: Why does a feather feel smooth one way and rough the other? Fish scales can feel that way, too. At the kitchen table, your child can compare animal coverings and use what they notice to sort pictures.
scenes.visual: Open on a schematic feather over a tray on a kitchen table. An arrow moves smoothly down the feather, then reverses as the barbs ruffle. A close-up photo card drawn schematically shows fish scales overlapping toward the tail. Animal picture cards fan out beside the tray.
scenes.narration: Why does a feather feel smooth one way and rough the other? Fish scales can feel that way, too. At the kitchen table, your child can compare animal coverings and use what they notice to sort pictures.

scenes.tts: This activity lets your child practice looking closely and describing what they actually feel. They make a guess, test it with water, and sort animal pictures by rules they explain. Formal group names like mammal or reptile can wait.
scenes.caption: This activity lets your child practice looking closely and describing what they actually feel. They make a guess, test it with water, and sort animal pictures by rules they explain. Formal group names like mammal or reptile can wait.
scenes.visual: Same overhead kitchen tabletop, pulled back slightly. Around the baking tray, three clean icon-like badges appear one by one in warm ink: a simple eye/hand sketch ('Look & feel'), a water drop with a checkmark ('Guess & test'), and three neat sorted card stacks ('Sort by rule'). The cards gently fan and settle; no photos of real children.
scenes.narration: This activity lets your child practice looking closely and describing what they actually feel. They make a guess, test it with water, and sort animal pictures by rules they explain. Formal group names like mammal or reptile can wait.

scenes.tts: Set out three to five craft-store feathers, fake fur, and two or three clean shells. Add a cup of water and a dropper. If you use raw fish, choose a piece with skin and scales still attached. Put it on a plate. Keep twelve to sixteen animal pictures face down nearby.
scenes.caption: Set out three to five craft-store feathers, fake fur, and two or three clean shells. Add a cup of water and a dropper. If you use raw fish, choose a piece with skin and scales still attached. Put it on a plate. Keep twelve to sixteen animal pictures face down nearby.
scenes.visual: On the kitchen table, arrange craft feathers, fake fur and clean shells on the tray. Set a small cup of water, a dropper and a face-down stack of animal pictures beside it. An optional plate slides in with a schematic piece of fish showing scales still attached to the skin.
scenes.narration: Set out three to five craft-store feathers, fake fur, and two or three clean shells. Add a cup of water and a dropper. If you use raw fish, choose a piece with skin and scales still attached. Put it on a plate. Keep twelve to sixteen animal pictures face down nearby.

scenes.tts: Stay with your child. Handle raw fish, scissors, and glass magnifiers yourself. Check shells for sharp edges. Use only craft-store feathers. Leave wild feathers where you find them. Keep small shells, small feathers, and loose dropper parts from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Use photos if anyone is allergic to a material.
scenes.caption: Stay with your child. Handle raw fish, scissors, and glass magnifiers yourself. Check shells for sharp edges. Use only craft-store feathers. Leave wild feathers where you find them. Keep small shells, small feathers, and loose dropper parts from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Use photos if anyone is allergic to a material.
scenes.visual: At the same table, an adult hand checks a shell edge. Highlight a small shell, a small feather and a loose dropper part together, then move them out of reach. Show the emergency number clearly as the narrator says it. Swap an animal-covering picture in for a sample to show the allergy option.
scenes.narration: Stay with your child. Handle raw fish, scissors, and glass magnifiers yourself. Check shells for sharp edges. Use only craft-store feathers. Leave wild feathers where you find them. Keep small shells, small feathers, and loose dropper parts from children under four. Call nine one one if choking. Use photos if anyone is allergic to a material.

scenes.tts: Have your child describe the feather, fur, and shell in two words each. Open and smooth the feather's edge. If you're using raw fish and have no cuts or sores on your hands, stroke it both ways. Keep hands away from faces and mouths. Wash your hands with soap and water immediately after touching fish, before touching anything else.
scenes.caption: Have your child describe the feather, fur, and shell in two words each. Open and smooth the feather's edge. If you're using raw fish and have no cuts or sores on your hands, stroke it both ways. Keep hands away from faces and mouths. Wash your hands with soap and water immediately after touching fish, before touching anything else.
scenes.visual: At the same tray, show the feather, fur and shell, with a pencil writing two descriptions beside each. Zoom in as the feather separates and its tiny hooks rejoin. If using the fish, show only the adult hand stroking the scales on the plate in both directions. Follow with a schematic soap-and-water handwash.
scenes.narration: Have your child describe the feather, fur, and shell in two words each. Open and smooth the feather's edge. If you're using raw fish and have no cuts or sores on your hands, stroke it both ways. Keep hands away from faces and mouths. Wash your hands with soap and water immediately after touching fish, before touching anything else.

scenes.tts: Before the water test, ask, "Which one will stay driest if it gets wet?" Place three drops on the feather and three on the fur. Water often beads on feathers, while fur and craft feathers vary. Each coat fits where an animal lives.
scenes.caption: Before the water test, ask, "Which one will stay driest if it gets wet?" Place three drops on the feather and three on the fur. Water often beads on feathers, while fur and craft feathers vary. Each coat fits where an animal lives.
scenes.visual: On the same tray, the dropper glides over the feather and releases three bright blue drops that gather into round shimmering beads. The dropper moves over the fake fur and releases three drops: one beads slightly while two gently darken and soak in, showing variation clearly. A subtle banner label above reads 'Guess, then drip'.
scenes.narration: Before the water test, ask, "Which one will stay driest if it gets wet?" Place three drops on the feather and three on the fur. Water often beads on feathers, while fur and craft feathers vary. Each coat fits where an animal lives.

scenes.tts: Flip the pictures over and match animals to their coverings. Look for legs, wings, fins, and tails. Ask, "Does it live on land or in water, and how does it move?" Sort by covering, then by leg count, then by movement. Let your child pick a fourth rule.
scenes.caption: Flip the pictures over and match animals to their coverings. Look for legs, wings, fins, and tails. Ask, "Does it live on land or in water, and how does it move?" Sort by covering, then by leg count, then by movement. Let your child pick a fourth rule.
scenes.visual: At the same table, flip over the animal cards. Match sample cards to coverings on the tray, then regroup them by leg count. Show sample movements with a dog walking, a snake crawling, a bat flying and a fish swimming. Leave space for the child's own sort.
scenes.narration: Flip the pictures over and match animals to their coverings. Look for legs, wings, fins, and tails. Ask, "Does it live on land or in water, and how does it move?" Sort by covering, then by leg count, then by movement. Let your child pick a fourth rule.

scenes.tts: A bat flies, and a penguin has feathers. Imagine your child sorts those two pictures by body covering. Before you turn the cards over, predict whether the bat and penguin will go in the same group.
scenes.caption: A bat flies, and a penguin has feathers. Imagine your child sorts those two pictures by body covering. Before you turn the cards over, predict whether the bat and penguin will go in the same group.
scenes.visual: Slide the bat and penguin cards beside each other at the same table, then flip them face down. Keep the feather and fur on the tray in view. Put the question above the cards in large type: 'Same covering group?'
scenes.narration: A bat flies, and a penguin has feathers. Imagine your child sorts those two pictures by body covering. Before you turn the cards over, predict whether the bat and penguin will go in the same group.

scenes.visual: Hold the face-down bat and penguin cards and the question 'Same covering group?' on screen through the silent pause.

scenes.tts: Turn the bat and penguin cards over. Ask, "Which one flies, and which one has feathers?" Bats have fur, and penguins have feathers. Put them in different groups when you sort by covering. The group depends on the feature you choose.
scenes.caption: Turn the bat and penguin cards over. Ask, "Which one flies, and which one has feathers?" Bats have fur, and penguins have feathers. Put them in different groups when you sort by covering. The group depends on the feature you choose.
scenes.visual: Turn both cards face up in place. The bat card slides beside the fur patch, and the penguin card slides beside the feather. Briefly highlight each covering on the cards so the parent can see what determines the groups.
scenes.narration: Turn the bat and penguin cards over. Ask, "Which one flies, and which one has feathers?" Bats have fur, and penguins have feathers. Put them in different groups when you sort by covering. The group depends on the feature you choose.

scenes.tts: Wrap and refrigerate the fish within two hours of taking it out. If the room is above ninety degrees Fahrenheit, you have one hour. If it has been out longer, throw it away. Wash hands with soap and water for twenty seconds. Wash the tray and table with soap and water.
scenes.caption: Wrap and refrigerate the fish within two hours of taking it out. If the room is above ninety degrees Fahrenheit, you have one hour. If it has been out longer, throw it away. Wash hands with soap and water for twenty seconds. Wash the tray and table with soap and water.
scenes.visual: Show the optional fish plate being wrapped and moved to a refrigerator icon. Show the shorter cleanup clock for a hot room, then move a plate that is past the time limit toward a bin. Finish with soap and water on the hands, tray and table.
scenes.narration: Wrap and refrigerate the fish within two hours of taking it out. If the room is above ninety degrees Fahrenheit, you have one hour. If it has been out longer, throw it away. Wash hands with soap and water for twenty seconds. Wash the tray and table with soap and water.
